summary: This standards-track document describes extensions to RSVP-TE for locally protecting the egress node or nodes of point-to-point and point-to-multipoint traffic-engineered LSPs. If the final node fails, traffic can quickly be handled by a backup.

eli5.summary: If the last stop on a bus route breaks, a spare stop is ready. This sets up a backup for the end of a path.

questions: how to protect the egress node of an lsp
what is a point of local repair
what is a backup egress node
subtitle: How an MPLS traffic-engineered path can survive the failure of its last router by switching to a backup egress.

tldr.problem: RSVP-TE already had local protection for transit nodes of an LSP, but nothing for the egress node, so traffic was lost when the egress failed.
tldr.mechanism: The ingress or primary egress names a backup egress, and the node just upstream of the primary egress (the point of local repair) builds a backup LSP to it, using an SERO with a new Egress Protection subobject. The primary egress shares service labels with the backup egress so it can deliver traffic the same way.
tldr.outcome: When the primary egress fails, the upstream node switches traffic to the backup LSP, and the RFC says this takes tens of milliseconds.

facts.label: Subobject types
facts.value: 1 to 4 (IPv4/IPv6 primary egress, IPv4/IPv6 P2P LSP ID)

today: RFC 8400 is a Proposed Standard that has not been obsoleted or updated. It extends the transit-node protection of RFC 4090 and RFC 4875 to egress nodes.

sections.title: The Gap in Local Protection
sections.content:
RFC 4090 describes two methods for locally protecting the transit nodes of a point-to-point LSP: one-to-one and facility protection. RFC 4875 shows how to use them for point-to-multipoint LSPs. Neither covers protecting the egress node of an LSP.

This document fills that void with extensions to RSVP-TE. Locally protecting an egress means that when it fails, its direct upstream node delivers the traffic to its destination through a backup egress node. Without such protection, the traffic is lost.
sections.eli5: The rules already covered what to do if a stop in the middle of a route breaks. They said nothing about the very last stop, and this fills that hole.

sections.title: How Egress Protection Works
sections.content:
The RFC's example has a primary P2MP LSP from ingress R1 to egress nodes L1 and L2. La and Lb are the designated backup egress nodes for L1 and L2. The backup LSP for L1 runs from its upstream node R3 to La, and the one for L2 runs from R5 to Lb.

In normal operation, traffic goes through R3 to L1, which delivers it to CE1. When R3 detects that L1 failed, it switches the traffic to the backup LSP to La, which delivers it to CE1. The time for switching is within tens of milliseconds. How the failure is detected is out of scope.

To set this up, an operator configures a backup egress node for each primary egress on the ingress node. The ingress sends a Path message that includes Secondary Explicit Route Objects (SEROs) naming the backup egress nodes. The upstream node of each primary egress then sets up a backup LSP to the corresponding backup egress.
sections.eli5: A spare path is built in advance from the second-to-last stop to a spare last stop. If the real last stop fails, the driver switches to the spare at once.

sections.title: The SERO and Its New Subobjects
sections.content:
The format of the Secondary Explicit Route Object from RFC 4873 is reused. For protecting a primary egress it contains three subobjects. The first names the branch node that originates the backup LSP, typically the direct upstream node of the primary egress. The second is an Egress Protection subobject, a PROTECTION object with new C-Type 3. The third, final subobject holds the address of the backup egress node.

The Egress Protection subobject carries E-Flags. Bit 31 ("egress local protection") set to 1 means local protection of egress nodes is desired. Bit 30 ("S2L sub-LSP backup desired") set to 1 means an S2L sub-LSP is desired to protect an egress of a P2MP LSP. Reserved fields MUST be set to zero and ignored on receipt.

Four optional subobjects follow, each with a Type, a Length and a body: the IPv4 and IPv6 primary egress subobjects (types 1 and 2) give the address of the primary egress, and the IPv4 and IPv6 P2P LSP ID subobjects (types 3 and 4) identify the backup P2P LSP tunnel using the egress address, a 16-bit Tunnel ID and an Extended Tunnel ID.
sections.eli5: The note that travels with the route has three parts: where the spare route starts, a label saying "this is for protecting the last stop," and where the spare ends.

sections.title: Roles of Ingress, Egress and Transit Nodes
sections.content:
The ingress MUST set the "label recording desired" and "node protection desired" flags in the SESSION_ATTRIBUTE object. It MUST include a FAST_REROUTE object with "one-to-one backup desired" or "facility backup desired" set, depending on the method wanted, and for S2L sub-LSP backup of a P2MP LSP it MUST set the matching flag in an SERO. The decision to create a backup egress can be initiated by the ingress or by the primary egress, but not both: a backup egress MUST be configured on the ingress if and only if it is not configured on the primary egress.

The primary egress, if the backup is configured there, MUST send a Resv message with an SERO. If the LSP carries service traffic with a service label, it sends that label to the backup egress as an upstream-assigned (UA) label, together with the related forwarding information. The backup egress recognizes a backup LSP by the Egress Protection subobject with the "egress local protection" flag set. It treats the backup LSP label as a context label and builds a forwarding entry for the primary egress from the UA label information.

A transit node that is not the upstream node of a primary egress MUST forward the SEROs unchanged. The upstream node (the point of local repair, PLR) works out the backup egress, computes a path that excludes the segment containing the primary egress, and sets up the backup LSP. If no explicit backup egress is configured, the primary and backup egress SHOULD share a local address, with a much higher cost on the backup, so they act as a "virtual node".
sections.eli5: Everyone has a job. The start of the route asks for protection, the last stop shares its secret ticket codes with the spare, and the stop before the last builds the spare path.

sections.title: Protection Modes and Local Repair
sections.content:
The PLR MUST provide one-to-one backup if that flag is set, otherwise facility backup if that flag is set. With one-to-one protection the PLR behaves as in RFC 4090, except the backup LSP goes to a backup egress in a session different from the primary LSP. With facility protection, one backup LSP MAY protect several primary P2P LSPs through the same PLR to the same egress, and the PLR keeps the primary LSP label in the label stack when it redirects traffic, unless that label is implicit null.

With S2L sub-LSP protection, the PLR sets up a backup S2L sub-LSP as defined in RFC 4875 and creates an inactive forwarding entry. On failure it changes that entry to active.

On detecting failure, the PLR follows Section 6.5 of RFC 4090 and SHOULD notify the ingress as it would for a transit node failure. It MUST keep the upstream part of the primary LSP alive by sending a Resv message upstream, and the downstream part to the failed egress SHOULD be removed. If only the link to the egress failed while the egress is alive, link protection is triggered instead; how to tell is out of scope.
sections.eli5: There are a few ways to build the spare path, but they all end the same way: when the last stop fails, the stop before it flips a switch and sends everyone to the spare.

sections.title: Example: Protecting L3VPN Traffic
sections.content:
An L3VPN is the typical application. CE1 and CE2 connect to PEs R1 and L1, with a P2P LSP from R1 to L1. R1 sends VPN traffic with an LSP label and a VPN label; L1 pops the LSP label and uses the VPN label to deliver to CE2.

The older ingress-protection solution needed a multi-hop BFD session between R1 and L1, an end-to-end backup LSP from R1 to La, a VPN backup label sent to R1 by BGP, and a VRF at R1 with two sets of routes.

With egress local protection, a BFD session runs between R3 (upstream of L1) and L1, which is closer and so may detect failure faster and more reliably. The backup LSP runs from R3 to La. L1 sends La the VPN label as a UA label, and La builds a forwarding entry in an LFIB for L1. L1 and La are virtualized as one node by configuring the same local address on both, with a lower cost to L1. R1 then needs only one set of routes. When L1 fails, R3 switches to the backup LSP, and La uses the backup LSP label as a context label to select L1's LFIB and the VPN label to forward the traffic to CE2.
sections.eli5: The spare stop learns the ticket codes of the real stop ahead of time. When passengers arrive there instead, it already knows which door each one needs.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 4090, RFC 4875, RFC 3209 and RFC 2205 continue to apply. Protecting an egress that carries service traffic needs out-of-band communication between the primary and backup egress nodes to pass the service label and forwarding information. The identifiers of the primary and backup egress nodes in the LSP should be verified to match those used in the out-of-band protocol, such as BGP.

IANA assigned C-Type 3 (Egress Protection) under the PROTECTION object class, Class Number 37, and created a registry of subobject types under it, with future assignments by IETF Review.
sections.eli5: The two last stops talk privately to share codes, so you must check that the stop you think you are talking to is the right one.
